issues.legal_issue: A person who neither carried a weapon nor fired it may be convicted of attempted murder through joint liability only if the prosecution proves that the person shared the principal offender’s common intention to commit that offence.
material_facts: The appellant and the complainant were quarrelling over a land dispute when the principal offender arrived while passing by and intervened.
The principal offender took out a pistol and fired at the complainant; the appellant neither carried a weapon nor fired it.
The injured complainant testified that the appellant urged the principal offender to kill him, but had not mentioned that alleged urging in his earlier police statement.

An eyewitness described the appellant’s words differently from the injured complainant, and another witness who confirmed the altercation and the principal offender’s conduct did not say that the appellant urged him to shoot.
The evidence did not establish that the appellant and the principal offender had arranged to meet at the scene or had agreed to kill the complainant before the firing.
There were existing land and family disputes between the appellant and the complainant, relevant to the court’s assessment of the conflicting testimony.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove a shared, premeditated or prearranged intention to kill, or that the appellant instigated the firing. The conviction was set aside and the appellant was acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code is a rule of evidence that gives effect to joint criminal liability, not a separate substantive offence. It applies where several persons commit a criminal act in furtherance of a common intention; participation in action and a shared intention to bring about the particular criminal result must be proved from the facts and circumstances. Common intention may develop during the occurrence, and an overt act by each participant is not required, but mere participation or a similar independent intention is insufficient. The court relied on B.N. Srikantiah v. Siddiah, AIR 1958 SC 672; Bharwad Mepa Dana v. State of Bombay, AIR 1960 SC 289; Harbans Kaur v. State of Haryana, (2005) 9 SCC 195; Manik Das v. State of Assam, AIR 2007 SC 2274; Abdul Mannan v. State of Assam, (2010) 3 SCC 381; Lallan Rai v. State of Bihar, (2003) 1 SCC 268; Ashok Basho, (2010) SCC 660; and Barendra Kumar Ghosh, AIR 1925 Privy Council 1.

rule.if: appeal_from_joint_liability_conviction and appellant_did_not_carry_weapon_or_fire and principal_offender_arrived_incidentally and no_evidence_of_prior_coordination and injured_witness_omitted_alleged_urging_from_police_statement and eyewitnesses_described_alleged_urging_differently

predicates.appeal_from_joint_liability_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction that attributes the principal offender’s criminal act to the accused through joint liability.
predicates.appellant_did_not_carry_weapon_or_fire: The accused did not carry the weapon used in the attack and did not fire it.
predicates.principal_offender_arrived_incidentally: The principal offender came upon the dispute while passing by and intervened.
predicates.no_evidence_of_prior_coordination: The prosecution produced no evidence that the accused and principal offender had coordinated their actions before the incident.
predicates.injured_witness_omitted_alleged_urging_f: The injured witness did not mention the accused’s alleged urging in the witness’s earlier police statement.
predicates.eyewitnesses_described_alleged_urging_di: Witnesses who testified about the accused’s alleged words gave materially different accounts of what was said.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a joint-liability conviction involves an accused who did not carry or fire the weapon, an incidentally arriving principal offender, no evidence of prior coordination, and the stated problems with the evidence of alleged urging, the conviction is set aside and the accused is acquitted.
